english.notes:
(i) Section 17(2) of the Act provides that A person does not breach subsection (1) by making a disclosure-
(a) to which any of subsections (3) to (8) of section 16 applies, and (b) which, in the case of a disclosure of customs revenue information, does not contravene any restriction imposed by the Commissioners for His Majesty's Revenue and Customs.
(ii) Section 17(3) of the Act provides that section 17(2)(b) does not apply if the person making the disclosure knows that the information was acquired otherwise than as the result of the exercise of a customs revenue function.
(iii) Section 17(4) of the Act provides that this section is also subject to any other enactment permitting disclosure.
(iv) Section 17(5) of the Act provides that in section 17(4) the reference to an enactment does not include an enactment contained in, or in an instrument made under-
(a) an Act of the Scottish Parliament,
(b) a Measure or Act of the National Assembly for Wales, or
(c) Northern Ireland legislation.
(v) Section 18(2) of the Act provides that it is a defence for a person charged with an offence under this section to prove that the person reasonably believed-
(a) that the disclosure was lawful, or
(b) that the information had already and lawfully been made available to the public.
(vi) Section 18(3) of the Act provides that a prosecution for an offence under this section may be brought in England and Wales only with the consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions or the Director of Revenue and Customs Prosecutions
(vii) Section 18(4) of the Act provides that this section is without prejudice to the pursuit of any remedy or the taking of any action in relation to a breach of section 15(1) or (2) or 17(1) (whether or not this section applies to the breach).
(viii) Section 10 of the Interpretation Act 1978 states that any reference to the Sovereign reigning at the time of the passing of the Act is to be construed, unless the contrary intention appears, as a reference to the Sovereign for the time being. As such, references to ‘Her Majesty’ and ‘the Queen’ have been replaced in the wording of the offences to state ‘His Majesty’ or ‘the King’, although this may not be the strict wording of the legislation.

other.penalty:
Either way
Summary: maximum 6/12 months imprisonment and/or a fine not exceeding the statutory maximum.
Indictment: maximum 2 years imprisonment and/or a fine.

The maximum penalty on summary conviction is 6 months for offences committed before 2nd May 2022; for offences committed on or after that date it may be 6 or 12 months depending on the general limit in a magistrates’ court, see section 18(5) and (6) of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009 and section 224(1) and (1A) of the Sentencing Act 2022.
On the 12th March 2015 the limit on fines imposed by a Magistrates’ court was removed – as such, the potential fine on summary conviction in relation to an offence committed after this date is unlimited.

Time limit for prosecutions:
None
